title: Waling
subtitle: The structural strengthening weave for basket upsets and rims
excerpt: A wale is a band of three or four rods worked in sequence, each passing in front of two or more stakes and behind one. The wale produces a much heavier weave than pairing, which is why it is used at structural points: the upset (where sides meet base) and the rim of every basket.

glossaryTerms.definition: A band of three or four rods worked in sequence, each passing in front of two stakes and behind one, producing a strong structural weave used at upsets and rims.
The upright structural rods of a basket that form the frame for the woven sides. Stakes are heavier-gauge rods than weavers.
A heavy flat-backed iron tool used to press woven rounds down tightly after each row.

content.text: A
wale
is a band of three or four rods that work in sequence around the basket, each rod passing in front of two
stake

s and behind one. The heavier structure of the wale compared to pairing (which passes in front of one and behind one) produces a thick, rigid band that resists lateral force. This is why the wale is placed at the base of the sides (the upset) and at the rim. What makes it work is the multiple-rod interlock: three or four rods crossing at different stakes creates a rigid lattice that the lighter pairing or randing cannot produce.
The three-rod wale

Insert three rods into adjacent spaces between the stakes. Call them 1, 2, 3 (left to right). Take rod 1 to the right: in front of stakes 1 and 2, behind stake 3. Take rod 2: in front of the next two stakes, behind the one after. Take rod 3: the same. Now rod 1 is the leftmost again; repeat.
The principle is: always take the leftmost rod first. It passes in front of two stakes and behind one. The weave spirals to the right with each rod.
The four-rod wale

Insert four rods into adjacent spaces. Same rule: take the leftmost rod each time, pass in front of two stakes and behind one (some weavers use in-front-of-three behind one for an even heavier band). The four-rod wale produces a wider, more pronounced band and is the standard for upsets in medium-to-large baskets.
Rapping and bedding the wale
After every round of waling, use the
rapping iron

to press the round down firmly against the previous one. Rapping removes gaps and compacts the weave. An unrapped wale leaves a loose band that allows the basket to flex at the upset, which defeats the purpose of the structural wale.
The upset wale

After the base is complete and the stakes are folded upright, the first waling round is the upset. The upset is three to four rounds of four-rod wale. Its job is to set the angle of the stakes (the flare of the sides) and to anchor the base of the sides to the base. A correctly waled upset cannot flex at the base-to-side joint; the basket holds its shape under load.
The rim wale

At the top of the siding, waling rounds set the final diameter and provide a firm base for the border work. Two to three rounds of four-rod wale is the standard. The rim wale must sit level all the way around; check by turning the basket on a flat surface and checking the wale line against the surface.
Joining in wale rods

Join each rod singly as it runs out. Replace it with a new rod of the same gauge at a butt join (new butt alongside old tip for four stakes). Do not join all rods simultaneously in the same area; stagger the joins so the wale remains even in cross-section.
